summary: The note argues that local economic growth depends on investment in education and human capital development, citing a skills gap between academia and industry and the need for lifelong learning. It calls for academia-industry partnerships, support for higher education institutions and start-ups, financial aid and accessibility measures, and stronger youth STEM and work-exposure programs. Quotes from business, political, and academic figures back these policy proposals.
one_line: Argues that local economies need strategic education and human capital policies, including industry ties, lifelong learning, funding, accessibility, and youth programs.
key_facts: A Global Economic Forum study released in late 2023 projected that by 2030 more than 1 billion jobs, almost one-third of all jobs worldwide, will be transformed by technology alone.

Michael T. Rochford, CEO of TechInnovate, spoke at the Local Economic Development Conference on October 12th and said, "The skillsets our companies require are evolving faster than curricula are adapting."
The World Bank's 'Learning to Realize Education's Promise' 2023 report advocates a continuous learning loop throughout one's career.
Sandra Linquist, a political figure, declared on November 8th, 2023 that policy should incentivize perpetual learning, from micro-credentials to online platforms.
Professor Emma Johnston, Dean of Springfield University, said on December 15th, 2023 that increased funding for infrastructure, research and development, and teaching resources is essential.
As of early 2024, start-ups like EdTech Innovations have begun emerging, illustrating the link between education and entrepreneurship.
Proposed lifelong learning measures include tax incentives for businesses that support employee education and subsidies for individuals seeking further training.
Proposed access measures include broader scholarships, reduced student loan interest rates, and pilots of income share agreements.
Working parents and rural populations are described as marginalized by traditional education models; evening/weekend classes and distance learning are suggested remedies.
For youth, the note recommends enhanced STEM funding, more emphasis on critical thinking, and internships and apprenticeships.
Lisa Chung, an educational policy advocate, addressed the Chamber of Commerce on January 9th, 2024, calling youth "future innovators, entrepreneurs, and leaders."
The note identifies a persisting disconnect between skills taught in post-secondary institutions and those demanded by modern industries.
